title: IndiGo Crew Member Kainoor Mistry Dies in Mumbai Cab Crash
excerpt: The 32-year-old cabin crew member, a mother of an eight-year-old boy, died of head injuries after her airline-hired cab crashed on the Western Express Highway — renewing scrutiny of outsourced crew transport.
body:
• Kainoor Mistry, a 32-year-old IndiGo cabin crew member and mother of an eight-year-old boy, died on Saturday evening of head injuries sustained when the cab taking her home crashed into a bridge ledge on Mumbai's Western Express Highway early Friday.
  • Police said the driver, 25-year-old Vijay Khose, lost control of the vehicle and have charged him with causing death by negligence; he was not intoxicated and did not flee the scene.
  • The cab was hired by IndiGo through a private third-party agency for crew transport, prompting colleagues and the aviation fraternity to question the vetting and safety standards of outsourced crew-transport vendors.
  • A similar crash in April 2025 killed another IndiGo crew member in Bengaluru, intensifying calls for the airline to be held accountable for how it moves its staff.

Kainoor Mistry was heading home to Mira Road from duty in a cab arranged by her airline on Friday morning when the vehicle rammed into a concrete ledge of a bridge on Mumbai's Western Express Highway in Borivali. The 32-year-old IndiGo cabin crew member suffered serious head injuries and, after two days on ventilator support at Bhaktivedanta Hospital in Mira Road, died on Saturday evening — leaving behind an eight-year-old son, according to police and colleagues.

The crash and the charges

The accident occurred in the early hours of Friday, September 18, on the northbound stretch of the Western Express Highway near Borivali East, a police official said. Mistry was the only passenger in a Maruti Swift Dzire. The driver, 25-year-old Vijay Khose, lost control and rammed into the ledge of a bridge, the official said. Khose escaped unhurt, did not flee, and — with the help of bystanders — transported Mistry to the hospital. Police said he was not under the influence of alcohol.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GnAH0LhwHn8

Police initially charged Khose with endangering life and rash driving. Following Mistry's death, they invoked Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — causing death by negligence — and issued him a notice to appear for investigation. Her funeral was held in Mumbai on September 20.

Questions over third-party crew transport

What turned a personal tragedy into an industry-wide debate is how Mistry was travelling: police confirmed the airline had hired the cab through a private agency to transport cabin crew. Friends and fellow crew members have questioned whether the driver was driving rashly, though police have made no official finding on that beyond the negligence charge.

Aviation workers on social media have pointed to a broader pattern — outsourced vendors, poorly maintained vehicles, drivers whose behaviour crew members say goes unchecked. One widely shared post asked why airlines talk about "girl power" while failing, in the poster's words, to keep a check on the third-party cab providers they hire. IndiGo had not issued a public statement as of Monday — a silence colleagues found galling, with one post circulating in the fraternity reading: "Her entire fraternity is at her funeral. IndiGo social media team se ek Rest in Peace nahi likha gaya ab tak!"

"An IndiGo cabin crew member, Kainoor Mistry, passed away yesterday following a road crash while returning from work in an office cab. Friends and colleagues say there may have been negligent and rash driving by the driver. In April 2025, too, a cabin crew member of IndiGo died in Bengaluru under similar circumstances."

— funeral notice circulated by Mistry's colleagues

A pattern, not an isolated crash

That reference to April 2025 has sharpened the anger: another IndiGo crew member died in Bengaluru last year in staff transport arranged by the airline. For a workforce that routinely boards cabs at odd hours between home and the airport, the question is whether crew transport is treated as a safety system or a cost line. India's aviation sector increasingly outsources crew transport to third-party vendors, and safety experts have long argued that fatigue, odd-hour duty schedules, and vendor oversight belong in the safety conversation — not just what happens inside the aircraft.

Why this matters for the diaspora

Millions in the diaspora fly IndiGo and other Indian carriers, and many work in aviation abroad as crew, ground staff, and engineers. Crew welfare and employer duty-of-care are global concerns: airline workers everywhere rely on their employers to get them home safely after duty. Mistry's death is a reminder that the journey to the aircraft can be as consequential as the flight itself.

What's next

Police said the investigation continues. The fraternity's demands are clearer: transparent vetting of third-party transport vendors, driver background checks, and accountability from airlines when outsourced logistics fail. Whether IndiGo breaks its silence — and whether the probe leads to systemic change in how airlines contract crew transport — will determine whether Kainoor Mistry's death marks a turning point or another entry in a grim pattern.
